title: Probability Theory and Statistics
summary: Probability in the first half (events, Bayes' rule, random variables, joint distributions, the central limit theorem) and statistics in the second (estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, linear regression read from Python output). Teaching is blended: before each lecture you watch a short video and do Grasple exercises, the lecture works through examples with polling questions, and the Dekking et al. textbook is the reference.

basis.description: The slides of all 16 lectures as text, the official CSE1210 course description, the four exercise sheets and the past papers. Time shares count content slides; bare title slides, wrap-ups and repeated animation frames are left out.
basis.caveat: From 2026-27 the course is CSE14A, renamed from CSE1210 with the content unchanged, still in year 1, quarter 4. The split between midterm and endterm has moved before: the 2024 endterm notes a shift since 2023, and the 2025 midterm included method of moments, bias and MSE. Chebyshev's and Jensen's inequalities are examined but barely appear in the slide text, so the slide count understates them.

topics.name: Probability rules, conditional probability and Bayes
lectures: Lecture 1 - Introduction to Course and Uncertainty
Lecture 2 - Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule
know: Sample space, events as subsets, and the definition of a probability function on finite and infinite sample spaces
Union, intersection and complement, the sum rule and the complement rule, and the difference between probabilistic and statistical reasoning
Permutations and combinations for counting equally likely outcomes
Conditional probability [[P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B)]] and the multiplication rule, also for three or more events
The [[law of total probability]] over a partition and [[Bayes' rule]], with prior, likelihood and posterior
Independence of two events and mutual independence of more than two, and why [[pairwise independence is not enough]]
do: Solve a test-and-disease or classifier problem with Bayes' rule, using a tree or a table
Compute probabilities such as P(A and B and not C) from a mix of conditional and unconditional facts
Check whether given events are independent
Use a probability tree for a sequential game, such as guessing boxes in a quiz show
pitfalls: Ignoring the base rate: in the teacher or park ranger example the description fits a ranger, but teachers are far more common
Mixing up P(A|B) and P(B|A), for instance the chance of a positive test given infection versus infection given a positive test

topics.name: Random variables, distributions and data summaries
know: Discrete versus continuous random variables; pmf, pdf and distribution function F, and how to get one from another ([[sum or integrate, difference or derivative]])
Bernoulli, binomial, geometric and Poisson; uniform, exponential, Pareto and normal, with their parameters and what situation each one models
Memorylessness of the [[geometric and exponential]] distributions
Using the standard normal table, including [[P(Z <= -a) = 1 - P(Z <= a)]]
Median and quantiles of a distribution and of a data set, the five-number summary and the boxplot
Histogram as an estimate of a density, the empirical distribution function as an estimate of F, and sample mean, variance and standard deviation
do: Name the distribution and its parameter of a described count or waiting time (number of non-sixes in ten throws, number of tries until success)
Sketch the distribution function of a mixture, for example a coin toss that picks between two uniform variables
Pick the most plausible model distribution from a five-number summary
Find a parameter from a given probability, such as the rate of an exponential from P(X <= 40) = 0.9
pitfalls: Drawing a mixture distribution function without its flat stretches and jumps, or letting it exceed 1
Using the wrong form of the Pareto or geometric distribution: in this course Par(alpha) lives on [1, infinity) and the [[geometric counts the trials up to and including the first success]]

topics.name: Expectation, variance and transformations
know: E[X] as a sum over the pmf or an integral against the pdf, and the [[expectations and variances of the standard distributions]]
The change-of-variable formula E[g(X)] = integral of g(x) f(x) dx, without first finding the density of g(X)
Finding the distribution function of Y = g(X) by rewriting P(g(X) <= y) as an event about X
Change of units: [[E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b and Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X)]]; standardising a normal variable
[[Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2]], the standard deviation, and degenerate random variables
Jensen's inequality: [[for convex g, E[g(X)] >= g(E[X])]]
do: Compute E[X] or E[X^2] for a pmf whose constant must first be fixed so the probabilities add up to 1
Find F_Y and f_Y for a transformed variable such as ln(X) or tan(X), and check E[Y] against the change-of-variable formula
Write a correct integral expression for E[g(Y)] without evaluating it
Use symmetry, linearity and Jensen's inequality to avoid long integrals
pitfalls: A sign error in integration by parts: the lectures show a 'wrong exam answer' where E[X] of an exponential comes out negative
Assuming E[g(X)] = g(E[X]) for a non-linear g

topics.name: Joint distributions, covariance and sums
know: Joint pmf tables and joint densities, and marginals by summing rows and columns or integrating out a variable
Independence of random variables: [[the joint pmf or density factorises]]; stochastic versus physical independence
E[g(X, Y)] as a double sum or double integral, and [[E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] under independence]]
[[Covariance as E[XY] minus E[X]E[Y]]], the correlation coefficient and how both react to a change of units; the [[variance of a sum adds 2Cov(X, Y)]] to the two variances
Convolution for the sum of independent variables, the [[gamma distribution as a sum of exponentials]], and generating functions for moments and sums
Covariance matrix, sample covariance matrix and the multivariate normal; a [[linear combination of jointly normal variables is normal]]
do: Fill in a joint pmf table that has given marginals and a given covariance
Find the constant, a marginal density and E[X] or Cov(X, Y) for a joint density on a square, triangle or half-disk
Set up the convolution integral for X + Y with the correct limits, and evaluate it at one point
Argue the sign of a correlation without computing it
Give the distribution of X - 2Y for independent normal X and Y
pitfalls: Multiplying marginals to fill a joint table when independence was not given
Calling X + Y normal because X and Y are each normal: that [[needs joint normality]], as the lectures' 'wrong exam answer' shows
Taking the convolution limits from one density only; they come from [[where both densities are non-zero]]

topics.name: Chebyshev, law of large numbers and the CLT
know: Expectation and variance of a sum and of an average of n independent copies: [[nE[X], nVar(X), and Var(X)/n]]
The law of large numbers, and why running averages of a Pareto variable with infinite expectation do not settle
Chebyshev's inequality [[P(|Y - E[Y]| >= a) <= Var(Y) / a^2]]
The central limit theorem for sums and for averages, and the rule of thumb for when n is large enough
do: Approximate the probability that a sum of 72 or 100 independent variables lies in a range, by standardising and using the normal table
Bound a probability with Chebyshev and compare the bound with the exact value
pitfalls: Standardising a sum with sigma instead of [[sqrt(n) times sigma]]
Thinking a Chebyshev bound above 1 is a mistake: it is correct, just useless

topics.name: Estimators: method of moments, bias, MSE and MLE
know: Model distribution, estimate versus estimator, and the sampling distribution of an estimator
Method of moments with one or two parameters, using [[the k-th moment E[X^k]]]
Bias [[E[T] - theta]], unbiased estimators, and how to rescale a statistic to remove bias
Mean squared error [[MSE = Var(T) + bias^2]], and comparing estimators by MSE
Likelihood and log-likelihood for discrete and continuous samples, and the maximum likelihood estimate
Properties of the MLE: [[asymptotically unbiased, asymptotically lowest variance, functionally invariant]]
do: Build an unbiased estimator from a count, a sum or a sum of squares, and compute its MSE
Derive a method of moments estimator, switching to the second moment when the first does not involve the parameter
Write down a likelihood, maximise its logarithm and plug in data
Find an MLE when the support depends on the parameter, such as U(0, theta) or a Pareto with unknown start
Say whether an estimator such as 2 times the mean or the sample maximum is unbiased or biased, and in which direction
Describe how to estimate an MSE or a sampling distribution by simulation or parametric bootstrap
pitfalls: Setting the derivative to zero when the support depends on the parameter: the lectures' warning example shows this fails
Forgetting that [[an unbiased estimator's MSE is just its variance]], and computing a long expression instead

topics.name: Confidence intervals
know: What a confidence level means, critical values z_p and t_(m,p), and how to read the t table
The studentised mean and the t-interval for a normal mean with unknown variance, with [[n - 1 degrees of freedom]]
Large-sample intervals without normality, and the interval for a proportion with its condition of [[at least 5 successes and 5 failures]]
Pivots: [[inverting a quantity with a known distribution]] to get an interval, also for non-standard cases
How width depends on confidence level and sample size, and choosing n for a required width
do: Compute a 95 or 99 percent t-interval from a mean and standard deviation, or from raw data
Build an interval for a scale parameter from given quantiles of a pivot such as S_5 / theta
Find the sample size needed for an interval of a given width
pitfalls: Using z instead of t, or n instead of n - 1 degrees of freedom, for a small normal sample
Using the 95 percent value when a 90 or 99 percent interval is asked

topics.name: Hypothesis testing and power
know: Null and alternative hypotheses, test statistic, significance level, critical region and p-value
Type I and type II errors and the power of a test, power curves and their link with effect size, alpha and noise
The t-test for a mean (normal or large sample) and the asymptotic test for a proportion
One-sided versus two-sided tests and their critical values
Choosing the sample size for a given power, alpha, effect size and standard deviation
Multiple testing with the [[Bonferroni correction alpha / m]], p-hacking, and the paired and unpaired two-sample t-tests
do: Carry out a t-test from a sample mean and standard deviation and state the conclusion
Compute alpha, a type II error probability or the power for a given rejection rule, also for tests based on a minimum, maximum or count
Compute a p-value from the distribution of a non-standard statistic, deciding the direction from H1
Find the n that gives a required power in a normal test
pitfalls: Taking the p-value in the wrong tail: decide first whether large or small values of the statistic support H1
Forgetting both tails when finding alpha or power for a two-sided rejection region

topics.name: Linear regression
know: The simple linear regression model, residuals, least squares and its link with maximum likelihood
Multiple regression with a design matrix and the normal equations
Categorical explanatory variables with [[k - 1 dummy variables and a base category]]
Sums of squares, R^2 and adjusted R^2, and why [[R^2 never drops when you add a variable]]
Residual plots to check the assumptions, heteroskedasticity, and transformations (a squared term, log of the response)
t-tests and confidence intervals for coefficients, the F-test for all coefficients, and reading Python OLS output
do: Write a model with dummies for a categorical variable and define each new variable
Compute how a prediction changes when explanatory values or the category change
Read R^2, the degrees of freedom, a coefficient's p-value or interval from OLS output, and build a 90 percent interval from the standard error
Decide from residual plots whether to add a squared term or transform the response
Decide which coefficients are significant, with a multiple-testing correction
pitfalls: Using k dummies for k categories, or not saying which category is the base
Preferring a larger model because its R^2 is slightly higher instead of checking adjusted R^2 and the p-values

prerequisites: Integration by parts and substitution, for expectations and distribution functions
Double integrals over triangles, discs and half-disks, for joint densities
Logarithms and derivatives, to maximise a log-likelihood
Infinite series such as the geometric series; exams give harder sums like 1/k^2
Matrices and matrix products, for the covariance matrix and the normal equations
Enough Python to read a regression output table
practical: There is no graded lab or project. Each lecture comes with Grasple exercises (instant feedback, plus four revision modules) and book exercises, and four exercise sessions work through exercise sheets whose answers are in the archive. None of this counts towards the grade, but the lectures assume you did the pre-lecture video and exercises.
studyAdvice: Estimation carries about a fifth of all points on the six papers analysed and appears in both halves: practise unbiased estimators from counts or sums of squares, MSE, and MLE when the support depends on the parameter.
Joint distributions have the most slides and are on every paper: drill joint pmf tables with a given covariance, marginals from joint densities, and the convolution integral.
Do the pre-lecture video and Grasple set before every lecture; the lectures build on them and do not repeat them.

Build your handwritten formula sheet week by week. The midterm allows only one side, so choose: the standard distributions with E and Var, the conditional probability rules and the computation rules for expectation and variance.
Learn Chebyshev's and Jensen's inequalities from the book: both were examined in 2024 although the slides hardly cover them.
Redo the 2024 and 2025 papers under time: several questions return almost word for word, such as E[X^2] from a pmf proportional to 1/k^4 and the joint table with a given covariance.
For the second half, practise reading Python OLS output; regression and tests on its coefficients were a third of the 2025 endterm.
